conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. My name is Maya Patel, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in supporting new mothers in the weeks and months after birth.

Over the next few minutes we’ll be using a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. It’s completely confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or re-word it so it feels manageable.

When we’re done, we’ll talk together about what the results might mean and decide on next steps that feel right for you. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

Most days I can still laugh—like when the baby makes those silly faces or when my husband tries to swaddle himself to show me how it’s done—but it feels flatter than it used to. It’s almost like I’m pretending to find things funny even when I do chuckle.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve been able to laugh, but it doesn’t feel as easy or natural as it did before she was born. Sometimes I catch myself smiling because I think I “should,” not because the joy just bubbles up like it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it was before. It feels more like I’m going through the motions rather than really feeling that spark of enjoyment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she spit up a ton right after I fed her and I kept thinking I must’ve done something wrong—like I held her wrong or ate something that upset her. My head knows it’s normal baby stuff, but I still feel like I should’ve prevented it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like I’ll be rocking her and suddenly worry that her breathing sounds different, even though she’s fine. It doesn’t last long—I can usually talk myself down—but it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just a quick rush of “what if something’s wrong?” and then it fades. I haven’t had any full-blown scares, just those little surges that leave me on edge for a minute or two.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. I’ll look at the pile of laundry or the sink of bottles and feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually push through, but it feels heavier than it should—like every task is one more brick on my back.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m tired enough that once I finally lie down I drift off pretty fast. Once in a while I’ll replay something dumb I said or worry about the baby and it takes maybe an extra twenty minutes, but that’s it.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—mostly in the late afternoon—where I just feel kind of flat and weepy. It’s not all day, but a few times this week I caught myself tearing up while folding onesies, thinking “is this my life now?” The sadness comes and goes; it’s not constant, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times. Once was when she wouldn’t settle and I felt like I must be doing everything wrong. It wasn’t an all-day thing—just a quick bout of tears, maybe five minutes, and then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wks post-delivery (self-report)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (reduced spontaneity of laughter/pleasure)  
- Intermittent low mood, tearfulness, “flat” affect (late-afternoon exacerbation)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant care  
- Unwarranted worries about infant safety, brief surges of tension without frank panic  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, “drowning” under chores  

Sleep / crying  
- Denies insomnia; occasional 20-min delay in sleep onset due to rumination  
- Two brief crying episodes this week triggered by infant fussiness  

Safety  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10); no suicidal ideation reported

Pattern summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present ≥ several days/week, not pervasive, no impairment of basic functioning, no safety risk. Findings meet threshold for continued monitoring and possible further evaluation for minor postpartum depression and/or anxiety.
